result.summary: The battle between Frogs and Mice rages on, with many killed on both sides, until the young Mouse Slice-snatcher arms himself and routs the Frogs. Zeus (called the Son of Cronos) pities the Frogs, hurls a thunderbolt after Hera's advice, and finally sends crabs who put the Mice to flight as the day ends.

scenes.title: Slaughter along the lake shore
scenes.summary: Frogs and Mice trade deadly blows with pebbles, spears and stones. Many fall, and Rueful alone among the Frogs shows prowess before diving away.
scenes.stakes: Warriors on both sides risk death in the fighting; the Frogs are losing fighters and fleeing.

scenes.title: Slice-snatcher arms for war
scenes.summary: Slice-snatcher is sent to war by his father, puts chestnut-husk armour on his paws, and drives the Frogs into the lake.
scenes.stakes: The Frogs face total destruction at his hands.

scenes.title: Zeus and Hera on Olympus
scenes.summary: Zeus proposes sending Athena or Ares, but Hera says they cannot help. He hurls his thunderbolt, which does not stop the Mice, and he sends helpers.
scenes.stakes: The Frogs are perishing and the gods must decide how to save them.

scenes.title: The crabs end the war
scenes.summary: Crabs arrive, nip off the Mice's tails and paws, and the Mice flee. Sunset ends the one-day war.
scenes.stakes: The Mice are maimed and routed.

alias_notes.explanation: Patronymic title for Zeus, used throughout the passage.
Pallas is a common epithet of Athena.

notable_quotes.reason: Closes the battle with a wry note that the war lasted only one day.

analysis.text: The poem parodies Homeric battle: tiny animals with comic names fight with epic formulas, and gods intervene as in the Iliad.
The parody draws on the Iliad's conventions, such as lists of the dead, divine councils and armour, and shows how familiar Homer was to its audience.

legacy.text: The Batrachomyomachia inspired later mock-epics, and was widely translated and imitated in the Renaissance.

fun_facts.text: The passage has a gap in the manuscripts, marked here as a lacuna after line 251.

language_notes.text: The comic names (Ham-nibbler, Pot-visitor, Water-larked) are translations of Greek speaking names that describe each creature's habits.
"His soul went down to Hades" is the Homeric formula for death; Hades is the underworld realm of the dead.
"A heavy burden for the soil" echoes Homeric phrasing about stones too heavy for ordinary men to lift.
Lacuna means a gap in the manuscript, where lines of the original poem are lost.
"Head-piece" is a helmet; here it is comically made of four pots.
The 'chestnut-husk' armour parodies heroic arming scenes; the husk is split along the joint to make greaves for his paws.
Pallas is another name for Athena, goddess of war; Ares is the god of war. Both are the usual divine helpers in epic battles.
Hera recalls Zeus's thunderbolt victories over Capaneus (struck down at Thebes), Enceladus and the Giants, who fought the gods.
'The cast the thunderbolt' is a misprint for 'then cast the thunderbolt'.
The crabs are described by riddling, epithet-like compounds without being named until the next sentence.
'One-day war' marks the war's brevity; epic battles often end at sunset.

context_notes.text: "Croakperson" is the translator's name for a Frog; the Mice and Frogs fight with reed spears, a mock version of heroic combat.
Ares was the Greek god of war, so the comparison gives the frog the grandeur of an epic warrior.
Son of Cronos is Zeus, king of the gods; Cronos was the Titan he overthrew.
Hera is Zeus's wife and queen of the gods. Here she says even Athena and Ares cannot help the Frogs.

literary_notes.text: The poem parodies Homeric battle scenes, using heroic flight and shield-dropping for tiny creatures fighting at a lake.
The graphic description of the spear thrust and gushing bowels borrows Iliad-style gore, which feels absurd on animals.
Comparing Rueful to Ares inflates a frog into a war god, while the pot helmet deflates the grandeur.
The only Frog to show prowess immediately flees, undercutting the heroic pose.
A tiny mouse is given the arming, boasting and divine pity of a Homeric hero, which makes the scene comic.
The thunderbolt that crushed Giants is used on mice and frogs, a deliberately oversized divine response.
Zeus's great weapon fails to stop the tiny Mice, undercutting the divine power of epic.
The pile of descriptive compounds mimics epic epithets while delaying the answer, a riddle the next sentence solves.
